items.followUp: Explain the steps involved in testing and debugging a computer program.

rubric.why: A solution plan gives an ordered method for solving the problem.
rubric.description: States that planning develops an ordered solution method.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that planning sets out the steps before coding.

rubric.why: Identifying the input, processing, and output helps define what the solution must do.
rubric.description: Identifies the input, processing, and output.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming the IPO components.

rubric.why: A planned solution can be represented in a suitable form before it is programmed.
rubric.description: Mentions representing the plan as an algorithm, pseudocode, or flowchart.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming a valid representation.

rubric.why: Checking the plan can reveal errors before writing the program.
rubric.description: Mentions checking or testing the planned solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing a test, dry run, or desk check.

modelAnswer: Planning a solution means deciding the steps to solve a problem before writing the program.
First, identify the required input, processing, and output.
Then develop an ordered algorithm and represent it using pseudocode or a flowchart.
Finally, check the steps with sample data to find and correct errors.

items.followUp: Describe two advantages and one disadvantage of a bus topology.

rubric.why: A star network connects each device to a central connecting device.
rubric.description: Identifies the central hub or switch.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming the central connecting device.

rubric.why: The central device provides the connection between the attached devices.
rubric.description: Explains that devices connect individually to the central device and communicate through it.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the connections or communication path.

rubric.why: A device can be connected or disconnected without changing the other links.
rubric.description: Gives the advantage of easily adding or removing a device.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this advantage.

rubric.why: A fault in one device or its link normally does not stop the other devices from working.
rubric.description: Gives an advantage related to faults affecting only one device or link.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this advantage.

modelAnswer: In a star topology, every computer or other device is connected by a separate link to a central hub or switch.
The central device receives data from a sender and forwards it to the intended device.
Advantage 1: A device can be added or removed easily without disturbing the rest of the network.
Advantage 2: If one device or its link fails, the other devices can continue working.

items.followUp: Explain how encryption helps protect online banking and messaging.

rubric.why: Encryption changes readable information into an encoded form.
rubric.description: Explains the basic conversion performed by encryption.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing readable data becoming coded or ciphertext.

rubric.why: An authorized recipient uses a key to recover the original information.
rubric.description: Mentions the key or decryption needed to read encrypted information.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this explanation.

rubric.why: Encryption helps keep personal and confidential information private online.
rubric.description: States that encryption protects privacy or confidential information.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this benefit.

rubric.why: Internet services use encryption to protect information sent online.
rubric.description: Gives a relevant everyday internet use of encryption.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming a valid use, such as banking, shopping, or messaging.

modelAnswer: Encryption changes readable information, called plaintext, into an unreadable coded form called ciphertext.
A key is used to decrypt the ciphertext and recover the original information.
It helps keep personal and confidential data private from people who are not authorized to read it.
Encryption is used in everyday internet services such as online banking, online shopping, and secure messaging.

items.followUp: What is the purpose of the INPUT and PRINT instructions in an algorithm?

rubric.why: SET is used to assign a value to a variable in an algorithm.
rubric.description: States that SET assigns or stores a value in a variable.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the use of SET.

rubric.why: An example shows how SET is used to initialize or change a variable.
rubric.description: Provides a correct example of SET notation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid example or a clear explanation of assigning a value to a variable.

modelAnswer: The SET notation is used in an algorithm to assign or store a value in a variable.
For example: SET total = 0.

items.followUp: Give one example each of volatile and non-volatile memory.

accept: loses data when power is off
loses its contents when power is off
rubric.why: Volatile memory requires power to retain its contents.
rubric.description: Describes volatile memory as losing data when power is switched off.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this property.

accept: keeps data when power is off
rubric.why: Non-volatile memory retains data without power; RAM and ROM are examples of the two types.
rubric.description: Describes non-volatile memory correctly or supplies a valid example alongside the distinction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct contrast or a suitable example.

modelAnswer: Volatile memory, such as RAM, loses its contents when the power is switched off.
Non-volatile memory, such as ROM, retains its contents even when the power is switched off.

items.followUp: Define a simple proposition and give an example of a compound proposition.

rubric.why: A compound proposition is made by combining simple propositions.
rubric.description: States that a compound proposition combines simple propositions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the defining idea.

rubric.why: Logical connectives are used to form compound propositions.
rubric.description: Names a logical connective used to form a compound proposition.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming a valid connective.

modelAnswer: A compound proposition is a proposition formed by combining two or more simple propositions using logical connectives.
Examples of logical connectives are AND, OR, and NOT.

items.followUp: Draw the truth table for the AND operator.

rubric.why: The truth table must include all four possible combinations of two input values.
rubric.description: Includes the four input combinations for P and Q.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for all four combinations: 00, 01, 10, and 11.

rubric.why: The OR operation is false only when both inputs are false.
rubric.description: Gives the correct OR output for all four rows.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for outputs 0, 1, 1, 1 in the matching row order.

modelAnswer: | P | Q | P OR Q |
